lead: A single-point cutting tool has a shank, a face, flanks, a nose and cutting edges. Its cutting behaviour is fixed by a small set of angles and a nose radius. Written in a fixed order, these numbers form the tool signature, for example 0-10-6-6-8-15-0.5. The signature lets a workshop grind, inspect and replace a tool without ambiguity. Lathe, shaping and planing work use such tools, so the signature is read every time a tool is issued.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for chip formation and orthogonal and oblique cutting, and 5.2 for force directions.

sections.h3: Tool parts and the angles that describe them

blocks.text: A single-point tool has six parts. The shank is the rectangular body held in the tool post. The face is the top surface on which the chip slides. The flank is the surface below a cutting edge; the end flank faces the end of the work and the side flank faces the machined surface. The nose is the rounded corner between the side and end cutting edges. The side cutting edge is the main edge; the end cutting edge is the short edge at the end.

items: Back rake angle: angle between the face and a plane parallel to the base, measured in the back plane. It controls chip flow along the face.
Side rake angle: angle between the face and a plane parallel to the base, measured in the side plane. It controls chip flow to the side.
End relief angle: clearance angle between the end flank and a plane perpendicular to the base. It stops the end flank rubbing.
Side relief angle: clearance angle between the side flank and a plane perpendicular to the base. It stops the side flank rubbing the machined surface.
End cutting edge angle (ECEA): angle between the end cutting edge and a plane perpendicular to the shank side.
Side cutting edge angle (SCEA): angle between the side cutting edge and a plane parallel to the shank side. It is also called the approach angle.
Nose radius: radius of the rounded nose, in millimetres.

Cutting edge inclination: angle between the cutting edge and a plane normal to the cutting velocity. It tilts the edge and sends the chip sideways; it is not one of the seven ASA signature slots. See 5.1.

blocks.text: Rake angles carry a sign. Positive rake thins the wedge and sharpens the edge. Negative rake thickens the wedge and strengthens the edge. Relief angles, ECEA and SCEA are positive.

The ASA system writes a single-point tool as seven numbers in fixed order: back rake – side rake – end relief – side relief – ECEA – SCEA – nose radius. Some syllabi call this the tool designation. The first six numbers are angles in degrees. The last is nose radius in millimetres on modern drawings; older shop drawings may use 1/64 inch.

The signature 0-10-6-6-8-15-0.5 means back rake 0°, side rake 10°, end relief 6°, side relief 6°, ECEA 8°, SCEA 15° and nose radius 0.5 mm. A minus sign before a rake value is part of the number. For example, −5-8-6-6-8-15-0.5 has back rake −5°.

The slots are not interchangeable. If a regrind note says 0-10-6-6-8-15-0.5, the grinder sets each value at its own slot. Reading 10 as back rake instead of side rake puts the wrong value in the wrong rake slot, so the wedge and the chip flow direction change. The relief values in slots 3 and 4 are unaffected. The fixed order lets a tool crib compare a worn tool with its drawing and identify a loose tool without measuring every angle.

The signature does not include cutting edge inclination. The ASA signature describes the tool in its normal setting. Inclination belongs to the cutting geometry of the operation and is treated with orthogonal and oblique cutting in 5.1.

sections.h3: How each angle changes the cut

blocks.text: Back rake and side rake decide how the chip leaves the face and how much force the edge carries. A positive rake gives free chip flow and lower cutting force. A negative rake gives a blunt, strong edge for hard or interrupted cuts. Too much positive rake makes the edge weak and hot.

Relief angles stop rubbing. A side relief of 6° keeps the side flank clear of the machined surface. Too little relief causes rubbing, heat and poor finish. Too much relief removes support behind the edge and invites breakage.

ECEA and SCEA set the shape of the cut. A larger SCEA spreads the cut over a longer side edge, so the chip is thinner and notch wear at the nose is reduced. Very large SCEA increases chatter and thrust force. ECEA controls the end edge; a large ECEA reduces end rubbing but weakens the nose.

Nose radius controls finish and strength. A larger radius smooths the machined surface and strengthens the nose. Too large a radius raises thrust force and causes chatter on slender work. A small radius leaves visible feed marks.

The practical rule is a compromise. Soft ductile work takes positive rake and a moderate nose radius. Hard work takes small or negative rake, small relief and a strong nose. The exact values come from the tool material and work material, covered in 5.4.

figure.caption: Each slot of the seven-element ASA signature sets one tool angle or the nose radius. Read slots 1 to 7 in the fixed order; slot 1 is back rake and slot 7 is nose radius.

examples.question: A single-point tool has ASA signature 0-10-6-6-8-15-0.5. Identify back rake, side rake, end relief, side relief, end cutting edge angle, side cutting edge angle, and nose radius. State the unit of each.
steps: Write the fixed ASA order: back rake, side rake, end relief, side relief, ECEA, SCEA, nose radius.
Slot 7 is 0.5, so nose radius = 0.5 mm, not 0.5°.
examples.answer: Back rake 0°, side rake 10°, end relief 6°, side relief 6°, ECEA 8°, SCEA 15°, and nose radius 0.5 mm.

traps: The seven ASA values are always in fixed order. Reading 10 as back rake instead of side rake changes which rake is which, and so changes the wedge.
A rake angle can be negative. Dropping the minus sign makes a strong tool look sharp and changes the force.
The nose radius is a length in mm, not an angle in degrees. It is the last slot and has no degree symbol.
Back rake and side rake are measured in different planes; SCEA and ECEA belong to different cutting edges. Do not swap their names.
Relief is not 'more is better'. Extra relief weakens the edge; too little relief rubs the flank.

quiz.q: Write the seven elements of the ASA tool signature in order.
quiz.a: Back rake, side rake, end relief, side relief, ECEA, SCEA, nose radius.

quiz.q: Why is the order of the seven ASA values fixed?
quiz.a: Each slot has one meaning. A fixed order lets a grinder, inspector or tool crib read the same numbers without labels. A number in the wrong slot changes the tool.

quiz.q: A tool has signature 8-4-5-5-10-20-1.0. State back rake, side rake, end relief and nose radius with units.
quiz.a: Back rake 8°, side rake 4°, end relief 5°, nose radius 1.0 mm.

quiz.q: A machinist grinds side relief 2° instead of 6°. Predict the effect.
quiz.a: The side flank rubs the machined surface. Friction and heat rise, finish worsens, and the edge may wear fast. Set side relief back to 6°.

quiz.q: What does nose radius 0.5 mean in a signature?
quiz.a: The nose is rounded with radius 0.5 mm.

quiz.q: Why is a negative rake used on hard work?
quiz.a: Negative rake makes a thicker, stronger wedge. The edge resists shock and breakage in hard or interrupted cuts, at the cost of higher cutting force.

quiz.q: Which signature slot holds SCEA? Give the SCEA value for signature 0-10-6-6-8-15-0.5.
quiz.a: Slot 6 holds SCEA. In 0-10-6-6-8-15-0.5, SCEA is 15°.

quiz.q: A tool with SCEA 15° is changed to SCEA 45° for the same cut. Explain the likely change in chip thickness and chatter.
quiz.a: Larger SCEA gives a thinner chip over a longer edge and lowers notch wear at the nose. It also raises thrust force and makes chatter more likely on a slender workpiece.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses ISO tool designations and insert shapes rather than a hand-ground ASA signature. Coated carbide inserts come with chip breakers moulded into the face, so the effective rake changes with depth of cut. Tool condition monitoring watches force and vibration instead of only the ground angles. Search next for ISO 13399 tool data, insert geometry codes, and chip breaker design.
